blocks.text: But for us birds there is an ancient law in the tables of the storks: that after the father stork, by feeding them, has made all the chicks able to fly, they in turn must feed their father. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: They in turn rear their mothers in old age. And Solinus: They have remarkable piety. For as much time as they have spent rearing their young, for so long are they in turn fed by their own chicks. And Aelian, book 3, chapter 23: Τρέφειν μὲν τοὺς πατέρας πελαγοὶ γεγηρακότας καὶ ἐθέλουσι, καὶ ἐμελέτησαν. κελεύει δ’ αὐτοὺς νόμος ἀνθρωπικὸς οὐδὲ εἰς τοῦτο, ἀλλ’ αἰτία τούτων φύσις ἀγαθή [Trephein men tous pateras pelagoi gegērakotas kai ethelousi, kai emeletēsan. keleuei d’ autous nomos anthrōpikos oude eis touto, all’ aitia toutōn physis agathē]. Storks are willing and eager to feed their fathers when they are old. Not that any human law compels them to it; rather, the goodness of nature is the cause. Therefore, when Croesus asked the Seven Sages, Τί τῶν ζώων εὐδαιμονέστατον; [Ti tōn zōōn eudaimonestaton?] Which animal was the happiest?, some answered Πελαργούς [Pelargous], storks, because δίχα νόμου τῇ φύσει τὸ δίκαιον ἔχουσι [dicha nomou tē physei to dikaion echousi], they observe justice by nature and without law. So Apostolius, Proverb 1141. And in Origen, Against Celsus, book 4, Celsus asserts that for this very reason εὐσεβεστέρους εἶναι τοὺς πελαργοὺς [III, 86] τῶν ἀνθρώπων [eusebesterous einai tous pelargous tōn anthrōpōn], storks are more pious than men. And Aelian, book 10, chapter 16: Αἰγύπτιοι τοὺς πελαργοὺς καὶ προσκυνοῦσιν, ἐπεὶ τοὺς πατέρας γηροκομοῦσιν [Aigyptioi tous pelargous kai proskynousin, epei tous pateras gērokomousin], the Egyptians worship storks, because they feed their parents in old age. And in the Hieroglyphics of Horus, book 2, chapter 55: Φιλοπάτορα βουλόμενοι σημῆναι ἄνθρωπον, πελαργὸν ζωγραφοῦσιν· ὑπὸ γὰρ τῶν γεννησάντων ἐκτραφεὶς οὐ χωρίζεται τῶν ἰδίων πατέρων, ἀλλὰ παραμένει αὐτοῖς ἄχρις ἐσχάτου γήρως, θεράπειαν αὐτοῖς ἀπονέμων [Philopatora boulomenoi sēmēnai anthrōpon, pelargon zōgraphousin; hypo gar tōn gennēsantōn ektrapheis ou chōrizetai tōn idiōn paterōn, alla paramenei autois achris eschatou gērōs, therapeian autois aponemōn]. When they wish to signify a son who loves his father, they paint a stork: for, having been reared by its parents, it is not separated from them, but stays with them right up to extreme old age, repaying them with care. Of the same kind is the fact that, to indicate that the force of justice lies beneath, ἐν τοῖς σκήπτροις ἀνωτέρω μὲν πελαργὸν τυποῦσι, κατωτέρω δὲ ποτάμιον ἵππον [en tois skēptrois anōterō men pelargon typousi, katōterō de potamion hippon], they carve a stork at the top of the sceptre and a hippopotamus at the bottom. So the Scholiast on Aristophanes on the Birds, and Suidas under the word Ἀντιπελαργεῖν [Antipelargein], which means to repay like with like, in the manner of storks; you may see it used in this sense everywhere by the ancients. Aristaenetus, book 1, Epistle 25: Οὕτω με νῦν ἀντιπελαργοῦσα δικαίαν ἀποδίδωσι χάριν [Houtō me nyn antipelargousa dikaian apodidōsi charin]. Basil, Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τινὲς τῶν εὐεργετημάτων ἀντίδοσιν ἀντιπελάργωσιν ὀνομάζουσι [Tines tōn euergetēmatōn antidosin antipelargōsin onomazousi]. Ambrose, Hexaemeron [col. 328] book 5, chapter 16: The repayment of benefits is called ἀντιπελάργωσις [antipelargōsis]. Refer to the same point what is found in the Porta coeli, fol. 30. d.: ואומרים מין עוף אחד שנקרא ללא״ק שמפרנסין אביו ואמו אחר שיגדל כמו שפרנסו אותו בקטנותו, They say that there is a species of bird named lalak (read לקלאק laklak) which in turn feeds its parents when they have grown old, just as it was fed by them when little. But whoever wants more on this subject should read Basil and Ambrose in those passages, Philo on the Decalogue, Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 25, Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, Philes, On Animals, chapter 6, and the paroemiographers Zenobius, Apostolius and Erasmus, at the words Ἀντιπελαργεῖν [Antipelargein] and Πελαργικοὶ νόμοι [Pelargikoi nomoi]. For we have no leisure to dwell longer on a matter so utterly hackneyed. I add only that storks show their gratitude not only towards their parents but towards anyone else, if Aelian's ^{b)} story of the woman of Tarentum, Heracleis, is true. When she had bound up a stork's broken leg and brought it back to health with her remedies, the following year the stork, mindful of the kindness received, dropped into her lap a stone by whose brilliance the house shone at night, ὡς εἰσκομισθείσης δᾳδὸς [hōs eiskomistheisēs dados], as if a torch had been brought in. I understand this as the lychnis, or lychnites, by which houses are lit up at night as though by lighted lamps. See Lucian, On the Syrian Goddess, and Pliny, book 37, chapter 7, and, what is most to the point, Philostratus, in whom πελαργοὶ καλιὰς οὐκ ἂν πήξαιντο, μὴ πρότερον αὐταῖς ἐναρμόσαντες τὸν λυχνίτην λίθον [pelargoi kalias ouk an pēxainto, mē proteron autais enarmosantes ton lychnitēn lithon], storks never build nests [III, 87] without placing the lychnites stone in them. Goblerus, in Gesner, reports that something similar happened at Wesel. There, namely, a stork that used to nest every year on the same house, after experiencing the kindness of its host for many years, on returning from its usual migration around the beginning of spring, threw at his feet, as if in thanks, a green ginger root, as a guest-gift and token of hospitality. Moreover the stork is also extremely φιλόστοργος [philostorgos] towards its chicks, and, if food to nourish them is not available from elsewhere, then, like the pelican, as they say, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ χτιζὴν (τροφὴν) ἀνεμέσας ἐκείνους τρέφει [tēn heautou chtizēn (trophēn) anemesas ekeinous trephei], it feeds them by vomiting up yesterday's food. So Aelian in the passage cited above. From all this it becomes plain to the reader that the name חסידה hasida, as if you were to say kind and pious, suits the stork for many reasons ^{(1)}.
